children: Markets have been volatile over the past few weeks as the leadership turmoil in Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) and rising oil prices have kept investors on their toes, with eyes keenly focused on inflation and what it means for the upcoming Federal Reserve policy decision.

However, on Monday, Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as CEO, President, and board member of the chipmaker, along with a recent pullback in oil prices amid growing supply, has given new wind to markets, sending benchmark indexes higher.
Despite the recent turn of events, markets are overwhelmingly predicting a rate hike from the Fed in December, as investors and experts believe inflation will remain a concern.
Why Ed Yardeni Thinks The Fed Should Raise Rates By 50 Bps

Ed Yardeni, economist and president of Yardeni Research, said in an interview with CNBC that the market reversal following Huang’s return may be a “one-day wonder” as other issues still weigh on the economy.
Yardeni cited political issues and artificial intelligence turmoil as factors that could influence markets going into next year.
“If you thought this was a rollercoaster year, it’s going to be even more so next year, especially on the political side,” he said.
The economist said that there is “certainly” a 25 basis-point hike on the cards; but he believes the Fed should hike rates by 50 bps.
He noted that while expectations of a rate hike have fallen, actual inflation numbers are steadily at 3% year-over-year, and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh “has pounded the table” about wanting it at 2%.
“I think they just need to do it. They probably should have done it in October, but politics was involved,” he said.
Meanwhile, data from the CME FedWatch tool puts the probability of a 25 bps rate hike in December at 96.4%, while the odds of a 50 bps hike are at 3.6%.
Falling Oil Prices Could Change Fed’s Inflation Outlook
However, some experts are arguing that the Fed should hold its horses, given the recent turnaround.

Robin Brooks, Senior Fellow in Economic Studies at the Brookings Institution, said in a post on X, “The fly in the ointment of yesterday's risk rally is that the Dollar kept rising. A strong Dollar isn't good for risk as it pulls liquidity out of global markets and EM suffers. Jensen's return can't fix the real problem, which is ill-advised Fed hikes…”
Meanwhile, James E. Thorne, Chief Market Strategist at Wellington Altus, also believes that Huang’s reinstatement and falling energy prices have brought some stability to markets.

“Now the energy shock is reversing, and fast. The 3-2-1 crack spread, the refiners’ margin, is now close to $ 38 a barrel, down from $ 79 in late September. West Texas crude is heading below $ 80, from $ 115 at its April peak. Wholesale gasoline is below $ 2.45 a gallon,” Thorne said in a post on X.

“When crude and refining margins fall together, pump prices fall faster than either. Gasoline at the pump is already down 15 per cent since September, to $ 3.81, and retail margins remain 30 cents above normal. More relief is coming,” he added.

Thorne said that he believes the Fed can tighten without raising rates by holding benchmark rates at 3.75% to 4% and “let the real rate do the work.” He cited declining oil and gasoline prices, lower PCE inflation expectations and recent market changes for his stance. The economist believes that these make a solid case for Fed rate cut in 2027.

“Huang’s return was the first step. Williams’s speech is the second. What is needed now is a Fed that is objective, apolitical and truly data-dependent. As energy falls, the data will say one thing: cut in 2027,” Thorne said.

All Eyes On PCE Report Next
The October U.S. Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE), the Fed’s preferred gauge for inflation, is scheduled for release on Wednesday.
Analysts expect the U.S. October headline PCE price index to rise 3.8% year-over-year and core PCE to increase 0.3% month-over-month, according to a Bloomberg survey.
How Are Markets Reacting?
U.S. benchmark indexes were mixed on Tuesday following a sharp rally on Monday after Huang’s return to Nvidia.

The SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) also declined by 0.48% in the overnight session, with sentiment in the ‘bearish’ territory.
One user said, “$SPY The Fed is nuts to raise rates now. What is needed now is to push oil prices lower and to drop the inflationary tariffs first. $QQQ.”

Another user said, “Everything is selling off now not because AI anymore but because tomorrow last important data for Dec FOMC and looks like we can’t escape hikes, we probably could repeat 2018, dec rate hike and tank all the way till Christmas And then bounce $SPY big drop.”
Meanwhile, the iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT) was flat amid ‘neutral’ sentiment.

title: Nvidia’s Rebound, Falling Oil And A Strong Dollar: Three Signals Complicating The Fed’s December Decision
